items.label: A
items.critique: Melodramatic, wordy plea with Nox humour ('the menfolk cannot live without us', the Ogres' stomachs grumbling); the 'choice' is accept or refuse, not two rival givers.

items.label: B
items.critique: Long, formal guard speech ('I surmise', 'despicable scoundrel', 'lose no sleep fretting about his soul') with distinct dead/alive rewards; the register is unmistakably the campaign's.

items.label: C
items.critique: Clean twin-giver template: honest giver names the place, the thief's 'Heh, heh' counter-offer, a tidy reward list; the 'priest will get another one' quip is well made but formulaic.

items.label: D
items.critique: Same skeleton as C and J (watchtower, 'Heh, heh', 'You never saw me, mate!'); the 'Halt! ... Oh, you're not one of them' opener is neat but too engineered.

items.label: E
items.critique: Warm and plain, but the precise hiding directions, the rival's 'Heh, heh' and the 'Don't tell [Person]' sting follow the same mould as the other new texts.

items.label: F
items.critique: The traitor's speech is long and precise ('a chest by [Person]'s bed, at the top of the watchtower', 'by the old elm south of the ford'); polished exposition rather than Nox's looser lines.

items.label: G
items.critique: Used-car-salesman gag ('only used it on weekends') with a concrete price haggle; quirky, short, and anachronistic in the way Nox's humour is.

items.label: H
items.critique: An absurd 50,000-gold sale of an inn and home, told plainly with 'lad' and a long rambling farewell; odd and specific in Westwood's manner.

items.label: I
items.critique: Bureaucratic sponsorship framing, apples, a 'foul little urchin', bats and a ruby key; meandering quest chain with concrete item handoff is very Nox.

items.label: J
items.critique: Third and fourth repetitions of the stolen-goods / turncoat template ('I rode with [Person]', 'Heh, heh', 'you never saw me'); well paced but formula-shaped.

tells: The new texts share one rigid skeleton: honest giver with precise hideout directions, a turncoat who says 'Heh, heh', and a cheeky closing line ('you never saw me').
New texts give exact locations and return points (north of the ford, by the old elm, here at the gate); Westwood's quests are vaguer and lean on gags.
Westwood's choices are often odd or comic situations (a used bow sale, buying an inn, a sponsorship) rather than a symmetric moral fork.
Westwood's register swings: formal Latinate words ('surmise', 'despicable scoundrel'), melodrama and anachronistic jokes; the new texts stay in an even, plain folk voice.
New outcomes list a tidy reward pair ('gold and these boots', 'potions and a little gold'); Westwood names sums ('500 in gold') or hands a key to the next step.
